newsitem.title: USA: Israelis, Palestinians struggle to save peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Israelis, Palestinians struggle to save peace deal.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian negotiators struggled into the night to save Middle East peace following a long working White House lunch between leaders who only days ago appeared to be edging towards war.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat met for three hours on Tuesday, pushed into a summit meeting by a U.S. president eager to stop gunfights and clashes unprecedented in three years of peace talks he helped foster.

The meeting, over a lunch of chicken and couscous, was surprising since the two leaders had met only once before for an hour at their border in September. Until recently the hardline Netanyahu had branded Arafat a terrorist.

Both sides said contacts were continuing but it was clear there were problems. A hoped-for, late-night second meeting which an Israeli official viewed as likely on Tuesday night had yet to take place by early on Wednesday.
Israeli officials briefing reporters throughout the day spoke of relaxed and comprehensive talks. But Palestinians were more cautious.
"All I can say is the talks are still continuing," Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah said late on Tuesday. "So far the Americans are doing their best."
On the only concrete point divulged by officials, Israel said it stood firm against U.S. pressures that it set a date to complete a long-delayed pullback from the West Bank city of Hebron.

Palestinians view Hebron, the last and most sensitive of the cities slated for handover, as a litmus test of Netanyahu's commitment to the peace deals he reluctantly inherited when he came to power at the head of a hardline government in June.
"In traditional Middle East diplomacy, the negotiators will work all night long and then sleep through the closing ceremonies," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, only half in jest.
U.S. officials hoped to hammer out a communique by the time the summit ended on Wednesday.

When they met, Netanyahu and Arafat not only shook hands, but they also sat for hours -- first with U.S. President Bill Clinton and Jordan's King Hussein and later alone with their aides over a long lunch in the White House library.
"It's been a positive start. The meetings have been constructive but by no means are we at the end of this process. The issues are daunting," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

Clinton called the summit in a desperate bid to prevent a collapse of the peace process following gunbattles and clashes that took the lives of 57 Palestinians and 15 Israelis in the West Bank and Gaza Strip last week.

Clinton was ready to rejoin the talks if needed. But he was never called and McCurry said that was just fine for the president who, leading in opinion polls five weeks before elections, saw his role as a facilitator.
King Hussein's contribution was to lend a kind of "moral authority," McCurry said. He said the king delivered "a very emotional appeal" for peace.
The king "talked about how he himself prays five times a day for peace and how all of the people in that room have that fundamental obligation," McCurry said.

Last week's Middle East fighting was sparked by Israel's decision to open another entrance to a tourist tunnel alongside Jerusalem's Temple Mount, holy to Moslems and Jews. But it also reflected Arab frustrations at what they consider Israel's slow pace pursuing peace accords.
Palestinians demand Israel close the tunnel, carry out the pullback from Hebron -- home to 100,000 Arabs and 400 Jews -- and ease a closure barring Palestinians from jobs in Gaza and the West Bank.

Netanyahu has toughened his stance since the violence erupted, accusing Arafat of ordering his police force to fire at Israelis the guns the peace deal provided. But a new opinion poll on Tuesday showed 80 percent of Israelis want him to press ahead with peace moves.
